items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Loko kuapā are coastal fishponds that Native Hawaiians constructed by enclosing shallow reef flats with stone walls.
• Each wall incorporated at least one mākāhā, a sluice gate containing a grate of closely spaced wooden stakes.
• Juvenile fish slipped through the gaps into the enclosure, attracted by its nutrient-rich water.
• Feeding on abundant algae, they eventually grew too large to squeeze back out.
• Caretakers could then harvest fish whenever necessary, even when treacherous seas made ocean fishing impossible.
items.stem: The student wants to explain how mākāhā helped keep loko kuapā stocked with fish. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Juvenile fish entered a loko kuapā through an open mākāhā, and caretakers then shut the gate so the fish could not leave.
Because caretakers could harvest fish from loko kuapā whenever necessary, the ponds remained a source of food even when treacherous seas made ocean fishing impossible.
The narrow openings in a mākāhā’s grate let small fish swim into a loko kuapā but trapped them there once they had grown fat on the pond’s algae.
A mākāhā’s grate admitted fish from the reef into a loko kuapā, where caretakers fed them algae until they were too large to fit back through the gaps.
items.explanation: The goal is to explain how the gates kept the ponds supplied. The notes give a chain: juvenile fish slipped in through the gaps in a mākāhā’s grate, fed on algae, and grew too large to squeeze back out. Choice C states that chain: the openings let small fish in and trapped them once they had grown.

A.why_wrong: The notes never say caretakers shut the gate; the fish stayed because they grew too large to squeeze back through the gaps in the grate.

B.recipe: OG (accurate, explains an advantage of the ponds)
B.why_wrong: It explains why the ponds were a dependable food source, not how the mākāhā kept them stocked; the gates are not mentioned.

D.why_wrong: The notes say the fish grew by feeding on the abundant algae themselves; nothing says caretakers fed them.

items.notes: Subject: history and technology (Hawaiian aquaculture); no researchers named, no web check (WAVE.md). Option fact check: A FALSE goal-shaped, D FALSE goal-shaped, B true but off-goal. Goal-only solve (without the notes): A, C and D all explain how the ponds were stocked.
band7_moves: how-goal over a three-bullet chain (enter, feed, too large to leave)
key states the derived link (the gaps admit small fish but hold grown ones) in words the notes do not use
two goal-shaped FALSE distractors that explain the whole stocking cycle with one wrong step: a gate the caretakers shut, and caretakers (not the pond) feeding the fish
one accurate off-goal option (an advantage of the ponds) built from the unused bullet

band7.why: Matches ee51ad04 and the section 5 EXPL recipe: a three-bullet chain (enter, feed, too large to leave), a key in words the notes do not use, and two goal-shaped FALSE options that run the whole stocking cycle with one wrong step deep in a clause (a gate the caretakers shut, which “sluice gate” makes plausible; caretakers feeding the fish). Goal fit leaves A, C and D; only bullet-by-bullet checking leaves C.

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); no named people or organisations

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Phytoplankton are microscopic organisms that absorb carbon dioxide during photosynthesis.
• In parts of the Southern Ocean, phytoplankton are scarce even though nitrogen and other nutrients are abundant.
• In 1990, oceanographer John Martin reported that phytoplankton in water samples from these areas, which hold very little iron, grew faster when iron was added.
• His iron hypothesis held that ice-age winds blew extra iron-rich dust into the ocean, fueling large blooms that removed carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
• Later experiments showed that adding iron to patches of ocean can trigger blooms.
items.stem: The student wants to provide an overview of the iron hypothesis. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The iron hypothesis holds that ice-age dust supplied iron that phytoplankton lacked, letting them flourish and draw carbon dioxide from the air.
Martin reported that phytoplankton in water samples from parts of the Southern Ocean, where iron is scarce, grew faster when iron was added.
Later experiments confirmed Martin’s proposal that iron-rich dust fueled phytoplankton blooms during ice ages.
Phytoplankton, which absorb carbon dioxide during photosynthesis, are scarce in parts of the Southern Ocean even though nitrogen and other nutrients are abundant there.
items.explanation: An overview has to state the hypothesis itself: ice-age dust supplied iron that phytoplankton in some waters lacked, and the resulting blooms removed carbon dioxide from the air. Choice A joins these parts in one sentence.

B.why_wrong: It reports Martin’s lab finding about iron and growth, evidence behind the hypothesis, but says nothing about ice-age dust or carbon dioxide, so it does not present the hypothesis.

C.why_wrong: The experiments showed that adding iron to patches of ocean can trigger blooms; they did not confirm what dust did during the ice ages.

D.why_wrong: It gives background on phytoplankton and where they are scarce but says nothing about iron, ice-age dust or the hypothesis’s claim about the atmosphere.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (oceanography). Real person and real hypothesis known well (Martin 1990, Paleoceanography; iron-addition experiments from 1993); no quotation used, so the famous tanker line is avoided.

band7.why: band_target 6. OVERVIEW with a close PART (B, Martin’s iron-shortage proposal without the dust or the carbon dioxide) and a FALSE overclaim of the later experiments (C): a strong band 6. Band 7 would need a second goal-shaped false option.

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); John Martin’s 1990 iron hypothesis and the later iron-addition experiments read as accurate; no invented finding attached to him
review.safety_fix: safety solve found B arguable (it stated Martin's 1990 proposal, a second statement of the hypothesis); bullet 3 and B now give his lab finding instead, D reworded to background only

items.subtype: Present the aim of a study
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• University cafeterias often encourage students to choose vegetarian meals.
• Some menus group vegetarian dishes in a separate section; others mix them in among meat dishes.
• Economist Nadia Haddad and colleagues wanted to determine whether this choice of layout affects how often diners order those dishes.
• Two campus cafeterias alternated between the layouts for eight weeks, recording every order.
• Vegetarian dishes were ordered more often when mixed in with the others.
items.stem: The student wants to present the aim of Haddad and colleagues’ study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Haddad and colleagues found that diners ordered vegetarian dishes more often when those dishes were listed among the meat dishes rather than apart.
For eight weeks, Haddad and colleagues had two campus cafeterias alternate between two menu layouts, recording every order.
Haddad and colleagues wanted to find a way to get university students to choose more vegetarian meals in campus cafeterias.
Haddad and colleagues set out to learn whether listing vegetarian dishes separately or among meat dishes changes how often diners choose them.
items.explanation: The study’s aim is the question the researchers wanted to answer: whether placing vegetarian dishes in a separate section or among meat dishes affects how often diners order them. Choice D states that question.

A.why_wrong: It reports what the study found, not what the researchers set out to learn.

B.why_wrong: It describes how the study was carried out, not its aim.

C.recipe: FALSE (background goal presented as the researchers’ aim)
C.why_wrong: Encouraging students to choose vegetarian meals is what the cafeterias often do; the researchers’ aim was to test whether menu layout affects orders.

items.notes: Subject: social science (behavioral economics). Researchers invented (Nadia Haddad); the design and finding are plausible and modest, attached to no real study or institution.

band7.why: band_target 6. An aim-of-the-study item with finding, method and background-goal swaps, the band-6 shape of 56b000d0 and c40a1964; section 6 check 2 keeps this goal at band 6.

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); invented economist Nadia Haddad reads as a real name; no real study named

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Conservators Lena Sjöberg and Tomas Ek examined three portraits long attributed to a Swedish painter who died in 1768.
• Using X-ray fluorescence, they identified the pigments in the white highlights of each portrait.
• Zinc white, a brilliant white pigment, was not sold as an artists’ paint until the 1830s.
• The first portrait’s white highlights contain lead white, a pigment European painters had used for centuries.
• The original white highlights in the second and third portraits contain zinc white.
• The first and third portraits are both painted on canvases measuring 60 by 48 centimeters.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize what a similarity between two of the portraits reveals about them. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Sharing a pigment that artists could not obtain until the 1830s, the first and second portraits were likely painted after the painter’s death.
The second and third portraits both contain zinc white, suggesting that they were painted decades after the painter’s death.
The first and third portraits are both painted on canvases measuring 60 by 48 centimeters.
Since the first and third portraits share the same canvas size, both were probably painted during the painter’s lifetime.
items.explanation: Only the second and third portraits contain zinc white, a pigment not sold as an artists’ paint until the 1830s, more than sixty years after the painter died in 1768. Choice B names that shared feature and what it reveals: those two portraits were probably painted decades after the painter’s death.

A.why_wrong: The first portrait was painted with lead white; zinc white appears only in the second and third.

C.recipe: PART (a true similarity with no significance)
C.why_wrong: The canvas size is a real similarity, but the option does not say what it reveals.

D.why_wrong: The third portrait’s original highlights contain zinc white, which was not sold as an artists’ paint until the 1830s, long after the painter died in 1768, so it cannot date from the painter’s lifetime; a shared canvas size says nothing about when either portrait was painted.

items.notes: Subject: arts (conservation). Painter left unnamed and conservators invented (Lena Sjöberg, Tomas Ek); zinc white’s arrival as an artists’ paint in the 1830s is known history. Review removed the conservators’ conclusion bullet (formerly last) and added an X-ray fluorescence method bullet after bullet 1. Option fact check: A FALSE goal-shaped, D FALSE goal-shaped, C true but no significance. Goal-only solve: A, B and D all state a similarity and its significance.
band7_moves: goal asks what a similarity reveals, so the key must name the significance
the significance is derived: an 1830s pigment against a painter who died in 1768; no bullet states the dating (review removed the conservators’ conclusion bullet, which stated it)
a second true similarity (canvas size) gives a similarity-without-significance option

two goal-shaped FALSE options: the right pigment on the wrong pair, and a lifetime dating drawn from the canvas similarity that only the third portrait’s zinc white, traced through two bullets, rules out

band7.why: Like 19b08ead the key names the significance of a similarity, and with the conclusion bullet gone that significance must be derived (zinc white, sold from the 1830s, against a painter who died in 1768). Goal fit leaves A, B and D; A fails only on which portraits hold zinc white, and D only once the student traces the third portrait’s zinc white to a date after the painter’s death. As drafted, the conclusion bullet stated the conclusion and killed D at a glance, which read band 6.

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); invented conservators Lena Sjöberg and Tomas Ek read as real Swedish names; painter unnamed
fixes: removed the conservators’ conclusion bullet, formerly last (that only the first portrait fits the painter’s lifetime): it stated the key’s significance and killed D at a glance
key B: dropped “unlike the first”, which only the removed conclusion bullet supported (lead white was used for centuries, so it does not date the first portrait)
explanation, D why_wrong and band7_moves rewritten to match
added a method bullet after bullet 1 (X-ray fluorescence identified the pigments in each portrait’s highlights), keeping the notes near the models’ length

items.subtype: Use a quotation to challenge a view
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Transportation agencies nationwide have widened highways in hopes of relieving congestion.
• Before one such project, state official Marcus Bell confidently predicted that the additional lanes would “give commuters back hours every week.”
• Economists Hannah Ross and Daniel Okoye compared highway expansion and traffic in hundreds of US metropolitan areas over two decades.
• Driving increased almost exactly in proportion to the new road capacity.
• Ross and Okoye concluded that added lanes “tend to fill up about as quickly as they are built.”
items.stem: The student wants to use a quotation to challenge the view that widening highways reduces congestion. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Before one highway project, Bell predicted that the additional lanes would “give commuters back hours every week.”
Ross and Okoye found that across hundreds of metropolitan areas, driving increased almost exactly in proportion to new road capacity.
Ross and Okoye, who studied hundreds of metropolitan areas, concluded that added lanes “tend to fill up about as quickly as they are built.”
Bell acknowledged that added highway lanes “tend to fill up about as quickly as they are built,” even as he predicted that commutes would get shorter.
items.explanation: The goal needs a quotation that undercuts the idea that wider highways ease congestion. Ross and Okoye’s words, that added lanes “tend to fill up about as quickly as they are built,” do that, and Choice C quotes them with their source.

A.recipe: NOQ (a quotation that does another job)
A.why_wrong: Bell’s words support the view that widening highways helps; they do not challenge it.

B.why_wrong: It reports the finding that challenges the view but uses no quotation, which the goal requires.

D.why_wrong: The words about lanes filling up are Ross and Okoye’s; the notes never say Bell acknowledged them.

items.notes: Subject: social science (transportation economics). All names and quotations invented (Marcus Bell, Hannah Ross, Daniel Okoye); the finding is the well-known pattern of induced driving, attached to no real study. QUOTE has no band-7 official items, so written as a strong band 6 (plan cell said 7).

band7.why: QUOTE has no band-7 official items (band-7 report section 1), so it cannot be band 7. Kept as a strong band 6 on e8494245’s pattern: a quotation doing the opposite job, an accurate paraphrase with no quotation, and a misattributed quotation.

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); invented Marcus Bell, Hannah Ross and Daniel Okoye read as real names; finding attached to no real study

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Freshwater lakes in cold climates can develop two distinct types of ice.
• Clear ice forms when lake water freezes directly, thickening downward from the surface.
• It contains relatively few air bubbles and frequently appears dark.
• White ice forms when accumulated snow becomes saturated with water and then refreezes.
• Filled with tiny air bubbles, it is approximately half as strong as clear ice.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference in how the two kinds of ice form. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Clear ice forms as lake water freezes directly, while white ice forms when snow saturated with water refreezes.
Because it is filled with tiny air bubbles, white ice is only about half as strong as clear ice.
Clear ice and white ice can both develop on lakes in cold climates, but the two form in different ways.
White ice forms when snow that has accumulated on a lake’s ice becomes saturated with water and refreezes.
items.explanation: To emphasize a difference in how the ice forms, the sentence must set the two processes side by side. Choice A does: clear ice forms as the lake water itself freezes, while white ice forms when soaked snow refreezes.

B.why_wrong: It contrasts the strength of the two kinds of ice, not how they form.

C.why_wrong: It says the two form in different ways without saying what the ways are.

D.why_wrong: It describes how white ice forms but says nothing about clear ice.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (lake ice). General knowledge; no named people.

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); no named people or organisations

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Viking shipbuilders in Scandinavia constructed both longships and knarrs from overlapping oak planks.
• Longships were used primarily for raids and warfare.
• Their long, narrow, shallow hulls allowed them to travel quickly and navigate far up rivers.
• Knarrs were cargo vessels that transported goods such as wool, timber, and walrus ivory across the North Atlantic.
• Their broad, deep hulls could accommodate heavy loads.
items.stem: The student wants to contrast the hulls of the two kinds of ships. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

Longships were used primarily for raids and warfare, whereas knarrs transported goods such as wool, timber, and walrus ivory across the North Atlantic.
Knarrs had broad, deep hulls that could accommodate heavy loads of wool, timber, and walrus ivory.
A longship’s hull was long, narrow, and shallow, built for speed, while a knarr’s was broad and deep enough for heavy cargo.
items.explanation: The goal asks for a contrast between the hulls. Choice D sets the longship’s long, narrow, shallow hull against the knarr’s broad, deep one.

A.why_wrong: It states what the two ships have in common, not how their hulls differ.

B.why_wrong: It contrasts what the ships were used for, not their hulls.

C.why_wrong: It describes only the knarr’s hull.

items.notes: Subject: history (Viking ships). General knowledge; no named people.

items.subtype: Describe a work to an unfamiliar audience
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Olga de Amaral is a Colombian artist celebrated for monumental woven works, many covered in gold leaf.
• In 2013, she introduced a series titled Brumas, Spanish for “mists.”
• Each Brumas piece consists of hundreds of cotton threads suspended side by side.
• The threads are individually coated with gesso and painted.
• Collectively, the painted threads create geometric shapes that appear to float.
items.stem: The student wants to describe the Brumas series to an audience unfamiliar with Olga de Amaral. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Each Brumas piece consists of hundreds of gesso-coated cotton threads, suspended side by side and painted so that geometric shapes appear to float in midair.
Colombian artist Olga de Amaral’s Brumas pieces are made of hundreds of painted cotton threads that form geometric shapes appearing to float.
Olga de Amaral, a Colombian artist, is celebrated for her monumental woven works, many of which are covered in gold leaf.
Colombian artist Olga de Amaral introduced a series titled Brumas, which is Spanish for “mists,” in 2013.
items.explanation: An unfamiliar audience needs to know who Amaral is as well as what the works look like. Choice B identifies her as a Colombian artist and describes the Brumas pieces: hundreds of painted cotton threads that form geometric shapes appearing to float.

A.why_wrong: It describes the pieces but never says who made them or who Amaral is.

C.recipe: OG (introduces the artist, not the series)
C.why_wrong: It describes Amaral’s woven works in general and says nothing about Brumas.

D.recipe: PART (names the series without describing it)
D.why_wrong: It identifies Amaral and gives the series’ name and start date but does not describe the works.

items.notes: Subject: arts. Real artist; only facts known well are used (Colombian fiber artist, gold-leaf woven works, Brumas from 2013 made of gesso-coated painted cotton threads).

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); Olga de Amaral (Colombian, gold-leaf woven works) and the Brumas series (2013, gesso-coated painted cotton threads) read as accurate

items.subtype: Introduce a concept to a new audience
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Time banking is a system in which participants exchange services using time, not money.
• Members earn one credit for every hour spent assisting another member, such as by tutoring or providing transportation.
• They can spend those credits on assistance from any other member.
• Every hour is valued equally, regardless of the task.
• Law professor Edgar Cahn popularized the concept in the 1980s.
items.stem: The student wants to introduce time banking to a new audience. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Members earn one credit for every hour they spend tutoring or providing transportation, and every hour of service is valued equally.
In the 1980s, law professor Edgar Cahn began popularizing the concept of time banking.
In time banking, a way of trading services without money, members earn credits by helping others and spend them on help in return.
Time banking values every hour of service equally, whether a member spends that hour tutoring or providing transportation.
items.explanation: Introducing time banking to a new audience means saying what it is and how it works. Choice C defines it as a way of trading services without money and explains that members earn credits by helping others and spend them on help in return.

A.why_wrong: It never names time banking or says what the members belong to, so a new audience could not follow it.

B.why_wrong: It says who promoted the idea and when, not what time banking is.

D.why_wrong: It names time banking and gives one of its rules but never explains that members trade hours of help for credits.

items.notes: Subject: social science (economics). Edgar Cahn’s promotion of time banking (time dollars) in the 1980s is known history; no other names.

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); Edgar Cahn, law professor, popularized time banking in the 1980s: reads as accurate

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Great Wall of Los Angeles is a mural painted along a concrete flood-control channel in the San Fernando Valley.
• It was designed by Chicana artist Judith Baca.
• More than 400 young people participated in painting it during the summers from 1976 to 1983.
• The mural extends approximately half a mile along the channel.

Painted during the summers from 1976 to 1983, the Great Wall of Los Angeles took years to complete.
More than 400 young people participated in painting Judith Baca’s Great Wall of Los Angeles.
The Great Wall of Los Angeles depicts California’s history all the way from prehistoric times to the 1950s.
items.explanation: The length of the mural is given in one note: it extends approximately half a mile along the channel. Choice A emphasizes that distance.

B.why_wrong: It emphasizes how long the painting took, not how long the mural is.

C.why_wrong: It emphasizes the number of people who painted the mural, not its length.

D.why_wrong: It emphasizes the period of history the mural covers, not its physical length.

items.notes: Subject: arts. Real artist and mural; length rounded to about half a mile; the dates and the 400-plus young painters are well documented.

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); Judith Baca’s Great Wall of Los Angeles (Tujunga Wash channel, 400-plus young painters, 1976 to 1983, about half a mile, prehistory to the 1950s) reads as accurate

Sedna travels around the Sun in an orbit that is extraordinarily elongated.
Sedna needs roughly 11,000 years to circle the Sun just once.

B.why_wrong: It tells when Sedna was found and where its name comes from.

items.subtype: Explain the origin of a name
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Kuroshio is a powerful current that flows northeast past Japan.
• Its warm tropical water raises temperatures along Japan’s southern coast.
• Its water holds few nutrients, so little plankton grows in it.
• Consequently, the water is unusually transparent, and its deep blue can appear almost black.
• The current’s name, meaning “black tide” in Japanese, derives from this dark coloration.
items.stem: The student wants to explain the origin of the Kuroshio’s name. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Kuroshio, the name of a powerful current that flows northeast past Japan, means “black tide” in Japanese.
The Kuroshio, or “black tide,” takes its name from its clear, deep blue water, which can look almost black.
Because it holds few nutrients, little plankton grows in the Kuroshio, leaving its water unusually transparent.
The Kuroshio carries warm tropical water northeast past Japan, raising temperatures along the country’s southern coast.
items.explanation: The notes say the name, “black tide,” comes from the current’s dark color. Choice B gives the name and ties it to that color: the clear, deep blue water can look almost black.

A.why_wrong: It translates the name but does not say why the current was given it.

C.why_wrong: It explains why the water is clear, not where the name comes from.

D.why_wrong: It describes the current’s effect on temperatures in Japan.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (oceanography). General knowledge; no named people.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Venice occupies a group of islands in a lagoon whose water is too salty to drink.
• The city has no freshwater springs or rivers.
• For centuries, Venetians collected rainwater in cisterns beneath the city’s public squares.
• Rainwater drained through stone grates and filtered through layers of sand before collecting in a central well.
• In the late 1800s, an aqueduct began delivering fresh water to Venice from the mainland.
items.stem: The student wants to explain why Venetians relied on rainwater for centuries. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Rainwater collected beneath Venice’s public squares was filtered through layers of sand before reaching a central well.
Venetians collected rainwater in cisterns until the late 1800s, when an aqueduct began delivering fresh water from the mainland.
With no springs or rivers and a lagoon too salty to drink, Venetians depended on rain, which they stored in cisterns beneath their squares.
Venice, which occupies a group of islands in a lagoon, collected rainwater in cisterns beneath its public squares.
items.explanation: The notes give two facts that together explain the reliance on rain: the lagoon’s water is too salty to drink, and the city has no springs or rivers. Choice C states both as the reason Venetians depended on rainwater.

A.why_wrong: It explains how the cisterns cleaned the water, not why the city needed rainwater.

B.why_wrong: It explains when Venetians stopped relying on cisterns, not why they relied on them.

D.why_wrong: It mentions the lagoon but not that its water is salty or that the city lacks springs and rivers, so it gives no reason.

items.notes: Subject: history (Venice’s water supply). General knowledge; the aqueduct date is kept to the late 1800s.

review.facts: no web check (WAVE.md, Rhetorical Synthesis); no named people or organisations

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The grotto salamander inhabits caves in the Ozark Plateau.
• Its larvae have fully functional eyes.
• During metamorphosis into an adult, its eyelids fuse over its eyes, leaving it permanently blind.
• The Texas blind salamander inhabits water-filled caves beneath San Marcos, Texas.
• Its eyes are reduced to two small dark dots beneath its skin, and it is incapable of seeing.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the grotto salamander and the Texas blind salamander. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The grotto salamander lives in caves in the Ozark Plateau, whereas the Texas blind salamander lives in caves beneath San Marcos, Texas.
The Texas blind salamander’s eyes are reduced to two small dark dots beneath its skin.
The grotto salamander, which inhabits caves in the Ozark Plateau, has larvae with fully functional eyes.
Like the adult grotto salamander, which lives in caves in the Ozark Plateau, the Texas blind salamander is unable to see.
items.explanation: Both salamanders are blind: the adult grotto salamander’s eyelids fuse over its eyes, and the Texas blind salamander’s eyes are reduced to dots under its skin. Choice D names both animals and that shared trait.

A.why_wrong: It contrasts where the two salamanders live.

B.why_wrong: It describes the Texas blind salamander’s eyes without mentioning the grotto salamander.

C.why_wrong: It gives a fact about the grotto salamander only, and its larvae’s functional eyes are not something the two animals share.
